_comment: Tunable DATA for the Engage skill (contributor RULE 3). Engage has two halves with very different risk. DETECTION (en_forms.py) is passive-ish page reading — it GETs the page and classifies its <form>s as login / register / reset by the FIELDS they carry, not by a URL word. ENGAGEMENT (en_engage.py) is the analyst deliberately creating an account on the operator's own box to see the panel/deposit/withdrawal/affiliate mechanics; it is OUTBOUND, ATTRIBUTABLE and IRREVERSIBLE, so it is gated. Every list below is what an analyst may reasonably want to extend for a new kit family WITHOUT editing Python: the tokens that name an identifier/password/confirm/referral/OTP field, the submit-button wording per form type, the anti-bot markers, and the engagement policy. Keys starting with `_` are documentation and are ignored by the loader. RULE 1 still applies: generic form/field vocabulary only, never a value lifted from a live case.

identifier_fields._comment: Tokens (matched case-insensitively as substrings of an input's name/id/type/autocomplete/placeholder) that mark a field as the LOGIN IDENTIFIER — the thing you type alongside a password. A form needs an identifier + a password to be a login; an identifier with NO password is usually a password-reset request. `tel`/`phone` count because many SEA fraud funnels log in by phone number, not email.

password_fields._comment: Tokens that mark a PASSWORD input. A field with type=password is treated as a password regardless of name; these tokens additionally catch password inputs a kit hid behind type=text (a known cloaking trick) or named oddly.

confirm_password_tokens._comment: Tokens that mark the SECOND password field of a registration form (confirm / retype). The presence of a confirm-password field is the single strongest tell that a form is a REGISTRATION form, not a login. Keep this list ahead of `password_fields` in the classifier.

login_submit_terms._comment: Submit-button / link wording that means LOG IN. Read from the button text, value or aria-label. Multilingual on purpose — VN/CN/RU fraud panels are common; add your kit's language here rather than in code.

register_submit_terms._comment: Submit-button / link wording that means CREATE AN ACCOUNT. Read the same way as login_submit_terms.

reset_terms._comment: Wording for a PASSWORD-RESET / forgot-password surface. A form matching these plus an identifier but NO password field is a reset request, not a login.

register_link_tokens._comment: Substrings of an <a href> (or its text) that point at the REGISTRATION page, so detection can follow ONE hop to find the signup form when the entry page only shows a login box. Word tokens only — the classifier confirms by reading the linked page's fields, never by the URL alone.

login_link_tokens._comment: Substrings of an <a href> that point at the LOGIN page — the reverse hop, used when the entry page is the signup form and you want the login surface too.

referral_tokens._comment: Tokens that mark a REFERRAL / INVITE / PROMO code field. Two reasons this matters: (1) a mandatory invite code is a base-rate tell of a closed fraud/MLM funnel; (2) the referral code an operator seeds their own ads with is a PIVOT — it clusters the funnel and sometimes names the upline. Emitted as a referral_param pivot when found.

otp_tokens._comment: Tokens that mark a one-time-code / verification field (email OTP, SMS code, 2FA, authenticator). Their presence is an ENGAGEMENT BLOCKER: a synthetic persona cannot complete an OTP without a real inbox/number the analyst controls, and the tool NEVER tries to bypass it.

captcha_markers._comment: Strings that, appearing in a <script src>, an element id/class, or an iframe src, reveal an anti-bot / CAPTCHA widget. Their presence is an ENGAGEMENT BLOCKER reported in the plan. The tool NEVER integrates a solving service and NEVER evades these — a UA swap is not a challenge bypass; a human decides whether to solve one by hand.

terms_tokens._comment: Tokens marking a 'I agree to the terms' checkbox on a registration form — recorded so en_engage knows it must be ticked, and counted as weak corroboration that a form is a registration form.

thresholds._comment: Scalars the classifier and the one-hop crawl budget against. `max_login_fields`: a login form is small — more visible fields than this (and a confirm-password or terms box) pushes classification toward registration. `register_min_fields`: registration forms ask for more. `crawl_register_hops`: how many linked login/register pages detection may follow from the entry page (kept tiny — this is detection, not a crawler). `fetch_timeout_s`: per-request timeout.

engagement_policy._comment: THE ENGAGEMENT GATE. Creating an account is NOT reading a page: it reaches out and touches the operator's own infrastructure from your egress, tells them a new member appeared at a known time, and cannot be undone — deleting the account later un-notifies nobody and the operator may have already logged the registration IP, fingerprint and email. So en_engage NEVER acts without explicit per-engagement confirmation, uses a SYNTHETIC identity only, and refuses to auto-solve a CAPTCHA or OTP. `require_explicit_confirmation` and `synthetic_identity_only` are ALSO enforced in code (the function signature), so a stale copy of this file cannot loosen them — editing here can only make the policy STRICTER. This is the same shape as BinaryPivot's ANY.RUN submission_policy.
risks: TIPPING THE OPERATOR — a registration is an outbound POST to the operator's own backend. They see a new account created at a known time from your egress IP, with a browser fingerprint, and can correlate it with the report that lands weeks later. On a small closed funnel a single unexpected signup is noticeable.

ATTRIBUTION / EGRESS — the registration and every authenticated page load originate from wherever this runs. Direct from the analyst's own network, that is a self-identifying beacon. Use a research VPS / VPN dedicated to the case; the tool warns hard and refuses a direct-egress engagement unless the analyst overrides it knowingly.

IRREVERSIBLE — you cannot un-register. The email, phone, password and persona used are now known to the operator; never reuse them on anything real, and never reuse a persona across unrelated cases (it links your own operations for the adversary).

LEGAL — creating an account, accepting terms and accessing a members area is a deliberate interaction with a live system. Do it only within your authorization for THIS investigation, and know your jurisdiction's line between OSINT engagement and unauthorized access / entrapment. This is an analyst decision, not the tool's.

VICTIM DATA — an authenticated panel may expose other users' data (chats, deposits, uploaded KYC, victim logs). Treat everything the account reveals as sensitive case material under the same handling rules as a stealer log; capture what is needed as evidence and no more.
POISONED VIEW — the members area served to a fresh no-deposit account may itself be a decoy; the real mechanics can gate behind a deposit. A thin panel is not proof the operation is thin.
try_first: en_forms.py on the target — the login/register surface, the fields required and the blockers (captcha/OTP) are read passively, no account needed.

Search the leak corpus for existing credentials to the panel (WebPivot IntelX / stealer logs) — a real operator or victim login recovered from a log answers 'what is inside' WITHOUT you creating anything or touching the box.
urlscan / Wayback for an archived authenticated view or an exposed API response someone already captured.
If a members area must be seen live, seek an existing account or credentials before minting a new one — a new signup is the most attributable option, not the first.
data_handling: Persona files and captured authenticated pages are case evidence — they live under cases/<case>/engage/, never in the skill.

Never put a real person's name, email, phone or document into a persona. The persona is synthetic by construction; if a real disposable inbox/number is wired for OTP, it must be one the analyst controls and dedicated to research.
One persona per case. Do not reuse it elsewhere — a reused research identity links your investigations together for the adversary.

The puppet-inbox pool holds REAL credentials to mailboxes the analyst controls. It is CASE/OPERATOR data (RULE 1): it lives ONLY in the git-ignored store (default knowledge/engage_inboxes.json), is referenced by PATH via ENGAGE_INBOX_POOL, and is NEVER written into the skill, a fixture, or a commit.

The mission material — the scammer's wallet and bank details, the service flow, the credential-harvester upload path — is high-value evidence and may sit beside OTHER victims' data. Capture what proves the flow and no more; handle it like a stealer log.
mission: Once inside, the objective is the OPERATOR's money and mechanics — the things the public page hides behind the login: the crypto WALLET addresses deposits actually go to, the BANK / payee account details, the SERVICES and FLOW the platform runs (deposit → 'trade'/'task' → withdraw-block → top-up demand), and the UPLOAD PATH of any credential harvester (where the panel POSTs captured credentials / KYC uploads).

Every finding is fed back into WebPivot + IntelAnalysis under the SAME rails — a wallet or account is base-rate checked and judged same-kit vs same-operator before it attributes anyone. A shared payment processor address is infrastructure, not the operator's wallet.

A wallet or bank account the operator collects on is among the strongest identity-bearing artifacts in the whole kit: it is reused across the estate and it is where a financial-intelligence / law-enforcement referral begins.
kyc_and_confirmation: Most fraud funnels do NOT verify identity — a made-up username + password registers, and you log straight in. Do that and skip the inbox entirely.

When a funnel DOES gate on email confirmation (or light KYC), the persona must use a REAL mailbox the analyst controls — one of the puppet-inbox pool. en_engage registers, en_inbox waits for the confirmation email and extracts the confirm link, the link is opened, then login proceeds.
en_inbox only READS a mailbox you own over IMAP — it never sends mail and never touches anyone else's inbox. It confirms the analyst's own account; that is the whole of what it does.
Hard KYC (government ID / selfie / liveness) is a STOP — the tool never fabricates or uploads identity documents. A human decides whether that engagement is in scope at all.

kyc_confirmation._comment: How en_inbox recognises the registration confirmation email in a puppet mailbox and pulls the link out. `link_keywords` are substrings that mark the confirm/verify URL among the links in the email body; `subject_markers` help match the right message; `link_path_hints` are URL path fragments a confirm link commonly carries. `poll_timeout_s`/`poll_interval_s` bound the wait. Matching is corroborated by the TARGET DOMAIN too, so an unrelated newsletter in the same inbox is not mistaken for the confirmation.

harvest_targets._comment: What en_harvest looks for in the AUTHENTICATED page — the mission. Keyword buckets that flag WHERE on the panel the money/mechanics live, so the extractor and the analyst know what a match means. These are context labels; the actual wallet/bank/upload extraction uses the pattern groups below.

credential_harvester_markers._comment: Signs that a page/endpoint is a CREDENTIAL HARVESTER — where captured logins/KYC are POSTed or stored. `upload_path_hints` are URL/action fragments that a harvester's collector commonly uses; `harvester_field_markers` are input names that mean the page is collecting third-party credentials (a victim's bank/exchange login), not the platform's own signup. Reporting the upload PATH is the point: it is the operator's own routing and it clusters the kit.

modal_dismiss_labels._comment: Button/label text (any language) that DISMISSES an interstitial modal blocking the form or the panel — a cookie notice, a 'link your Telegram' nag, a payment-notice overlay, a warmup splash. en_engage clicks the first match inside the top-most [role=dialog] before it interacts, because a React SPA commonly floats one of these over the auth/deposit view and it silently intercepts every click (observed on a live VN fraud panel: registration and the deposit walk both stalled on an aria-modal overlay). NEVER a 'confirm payment' / 'submit' button — only close/skip/later/understood wording. It never solves a CAPTCHA (that is a separate, hard stop).

wallet_base_rate_exclude._comment: Addresses that are INFRASTRUCTURE, not an operator's wallet, and must NEVER be clustered on even though they match a wallet regex. The classic trap: a USDT deposit UI shows the operator's deposit `wallet` AND the Tether TOKEN CONTRACT address, and a naive sweep grabs both — the contract is in every USDT-on-Tron interface on earth. When an API response labels a field `contract`/`token`/`tokenAddress`, that value is excluded automatically; this list catches the same addresses when they appear only in the DOM. Extend it as new token-contract / router / burn addresses recur across cases.

api_wallet_fields._comment: JSON field names whose VALUE is an operator wallet/payment address to harvest from a captured API response (en_harvest.harvest_api). `wallet`/`address`/`deposit_address` are the operator's; `contract`/`token`/`tokenAddress` are the base-rate token contract and are recorded as EXCLUDED, never clustered. Field names are matched case-insensitively.

wallet_patterns._comment: Regexes for crypto wallet addresses to pull off the authenticated deposit page (the scammer's collection wallets). Deliberately anchored to reduce false positives; a match is still base-rate checked before it is treated as the operator's own wallet (a shared processor address is infrastructure). BTC (legacy/segwit + bech32), ETH/BEP20/ERC20 (0x), TRON (T...), and a broad USDT-on-tron note lives in wallet_context above.

bank_patterns._comment: Regexes for banking details on the authenticated payout/deposit page (the scammer's payee account). IBAN is well-structured; SWIFT/BIC is 8 or 11 alnum; a bare account number is intentionally NOT a blind regex (too many false positives) — it is captured by proximity to the bank_context keywords above instead. Every hit is corroborated against the bank_context label, never clustered on a raw number alone.
